title: Teach what you know
tomorrow: Saba's old Chumash is full of pencil notes. who writes in a holy book?

cards: The kitchen table, late. A younger cousin, a printout of his bar mitzvah portion, and a phone leaning on the fruit bowl, playing a recording he's supposed to copy. He looks up.
You did this, right? Can you just teach me? The honest answer is: sort of.
You did it once. Some of it stuck. The Talmud tells about a teacher whose student needed every lesson said again and again.
And one day, even that wasn't enough.

teach.b: The teacher is Rabbi Preida, in the tractate Eruvin. His student learned each lesson only after hearing it four hundred times, so Rabbi Preida said it four hundred times.
One day he was needed somewhere else, for a good deed. He taught the lesson four hundred times, and the student didn't get it. What's different today? he asked.
The student said: since they called you, my mind's been on the door, waiting for you to leave. So the rabbi said: pay attention. And he taught it four hundred times more.
The Talmud says a voice from heaven then offered him a choice of rewards, and he chose the one his whole generation could share. Pirkei Avot puts the idea in one line.
Rabbi Ishmael, son of Rabbi Yose, says: one who learns in order to teach is given the means both to learn and to teach. Teaching isn't the prize at the end of learning. It's how learning finishes.

teach.h: FROM MY STUDENTS, MOST OF ALL.
teach.b: Rabbi Chanina says it from the other side, in the Talmud: much I learned from my teachers, more from my friends, and from my students most of all.
Something to tell a friend tonight: in that story, the lesson is the teacher's patience, not the student's speed.
You don't need to know everything to teach. You need one thing you know, and the patience to say it again.

how: In Jewish study, learners often take turns explaining a text to a partner, and a bar or bat mitzvah student may be tutored by a teacher, an older student or a relative.

games.q: what does “teach what you know” mean?
o: passing on what you've learned, which finishes the learning
leaving all teaching to rabbis and trained teachers
waiting to teach until you've mastered the whole text

games.q: who said what about teaching — tap the pairs.
p: taught it four hundred times more
had his mind on the door
from my students, most of all

s: you have to be an expert before you can teach
Avot ties teaching to learning: one who learns in order to teach is given the means to do both.
in the Talmud story, the student finally learned because the teacher went faster
he went the other way: he asked what was different that day, then taught it four hundred times more.
a sage in the Talmud says he learned most from his students
Rabbi Chanina: much from my teachers, more from my friends, most from my students.

games.q: a kid you're tutoring keeps missing the same line. you've gone over it again and again, and you're running late. what would Rabbi Preida do?
o: ask what's pulling his mind away, then go over it again.
send him the recording; he'll learn faster on his own.
tell him it's fine to skip that line on the big day.
games.why: Rabbi Preida asked what was different that day, learned the student was watching the door, and taught it four hundred times more.

practice: Choose one thing you really know: a blessing, a family recipe, a story from these lessons, how to fix a bike chain. Quietly, out loud, explain it to someone who isn't there, as simply as you can.
Where you stumble is the part you're still learning.

wordCard.voice: Teach what you know: Rabbi Ishmael's line, lived. You learn in order to teach, and the teaching finishes the learning.

orig.note: Hebrew: to teach. Avot's phrase is ha-lomed al menat lelamed: one who learns in order to teach.

carryVoice: Your line: teach it. Rabbi Preida said it four hundred times more. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:5 (4:6 in some editions): Rabbi Ishmael son of Rabbi Yose, one who learns in order to teach is given the means to learn and to teach
Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 54b (Rabbi Preida and his student)
Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 7a (Rabbi Chanina: from my students most of all)
